issues.line_text: I came here because she needed someone to blame.
issues.description: Chapter title/opening line uses investigator language. 'Someone to blame' reveals Eleanor is seeking accountability for a crime, not hunting prey. Predators don't need someone to 'blame'ΓÇöthey need victims. This phrase positions Eleanor as someone seeking justice/closure, which spoils the reveal that she's Lily's sister investigating her murder.
issues.fix: I came here because he had to be stopped.
issues.rationale: Predatory language. 'Had to be stopped' implies Josh is a threat she's neutralizing, maintaining the misdirection that Eleanor is dangerous. Removes the justice-seeking frame without introducing new spoilers.

issues.line_text: I needed to take the pills. But not too manyΓÇöhad to stay sharp for what was coming. Josh had found the cameras. Found everything. This was the moment I'd been preparing for.
issues.description: 'The moment I'd been preparing for' is classic investigator languageΓÇöimplies a planned confrontation to reveal evidence/truth. Predators don't 'prepare for moments'ΓÇöthey strike when ready. This reveals Eleanor has an investigative endgame, spoiling her true role.
issues.fix: I needed to take the pills. But not too manyΓÇöhad to stay sharp for what was coming. Josh had found the cameras. Found everything. This was the moment everything would break.
issues.rationale: 'Everything would break' is ambiguousΓÇöcould mean her plan to hurt him falls apart, or their relationship shatters. Removes the investigative 'preparation' frame while maintaining tension.

issues.line_text:
I had to finish this. Now. Before I lost my chance.

issues.fix:
I had to end this. Now. Before I fell apart completely.

Before I couldn't finish what I started.
issues.rationale: 'End this' is more terminal/predatory. 'Fell apart' ties to her physical deterioration (pills just mentioned). 'Finish what I started' is vague enough to read as violent intent while actually referring to her investigation.

issues.line_text: Deep winter already, and the isolation was showing cracks. All three cameras. Every single one I'd placed. He'd found everything I'd been using to... to what? Watch him? Understand him? Prove something I wasn't even sure of?
issues.description: 'Prove something' is investigator languageΓÇöpredators don't need to prove things, they act on certainty. The self-questioning ('I wasn't even sure of') undermines the predatory certainty Eleanor must project in Acts 1-2.
issues.fix: Deep winter already, and the isolation was showing cracks. All three cameras. Every single one I'd placed. He'd found everything I'd been using to watch him. To see what he'd do when he thought no one was looking.
issues.rationale: Removes 'prove' and uncertainty. 'See what he'd do' maintains predatory observation without revealing investigative intent. Predators watch for vulnerability/opportunity, not proof.

issues.line_text: I should tell him. Should lay it all out. But looking at himΓÇöat the suspicion building behind his eyes, at the way he's already pulling backΓÇöI knew he wouldn't believe me. Not yet. Not without seeing the proof himself.
issues.description: 'The proof' reveals Eleanor has evidence to show JoshΓÇöinvestigator behavior. Predators don't worry about whether victims will 'believe' them or need 'proof.'
issues.fix: I should tell him. Should lay it all out. But looking at himΓÇöat the suspicion building behind his eyes, at the way he's already pulling backΓÇöI knew it would only make things worse. Not yet. Not while he was still fighting me.
issues.rationale: 'Make things worse' is ambiguousΓÇöcould mean escalate conflict or ruin her plans. 'Still fighting me' positions Josh as resisting her control (predatory frame) rather than needing to see evidence (investigative frame).

issues.line_text: The irony was staggering. He thought I was trying to frame him, when I was actually trying to save him from himself.
issues.description: 'Save him from himself' is completely antithetical to predatory intent. This is investigator/grief languageΓÇöreveals Eleanor's true protective/justice-seeking motivation, spoiling the misdirection.
issues.fix: The irony was staggering. He thought I was trying to frame him, when I was actually trying to make him see what he really was.

issues.line_text: I'd tried to tell him. Tried to show him who he really was. And he'd rejected it completely.
issues.description: 'Show him who he really was' explicitly reveals Eleanor's investigative goalΓÇöexposing Josh's true nature. This is investigator language that spoils her role as Lily's sister seeking to prove Josh is the killer.
issues.fix: I'd tried to push him. Tried to break through that wall he'd built. And he'd only reinforced it.
issues.rationale: 'Push him' and 'break through' can read as psychological manipulation (predatory gaslighting). 'Reinforced the wall' shows Josh resisting her control, maintaining the predator-prey dynamic.

issues.line_text: Of course he had. It's easier to believe I'm the threat. Easier to make me the villain in his story. The mind will do anything to protect itself from uncertainty.
issues.description: Eleanor analyzing Josh's psychology in clinical terms ('The mind will do anything to protect itself') is investigator/analyst language. The framing positions Eleanor as understanding Josh's denial of truthΓÇöreveals she HAS truth to reveal.
issues.fix: Of course he had. It's easier to believe I'm the threat. Easier to make me the villain in his story than to face what he was really afraid of.
issues.rationale: 'What he was really afraid of' is ambiguousΓÇöreaders think Josh fears Eleanor (predatory threat). Actually refers to his fugue states. Removes clinical analysis while maintaining psychological pressure.

issues.line_text: How had I become someone who couldn't separate truth from suspicion anymore?
issues.description: 'Truth from suspicion' reveals Eleanor has been seeking truthΓÇöinvestigator motivation. Predators don't struggle with truth vs. suspicion; they act on desire/compulsion.
issues.fix: How had I become someone who couldn't separate what I wanted from what I needed anymore?
issues.rationale: 'Want vs. need' is ambiguousΓÇöcould reference her desire to hurt Josh vs. need to finish her plan (predatory read) or her emotional attachment vs. mission (actual meaning). Removes truth-seeking language.

issues.line_text: I walked through the mansion turning off lights. Collecting the cameras Josh had found. Straightening the furniture we'd knocked over. Erasing the physical traces of what had happened while the emotional wreckage remained.
issues.description: 'Erasing the physical traces' explicitly frames Eleanor as covering up evidenceΓÇöinvestigator behavior protecting a crime scene or surveillance operation. This language reveals she's operating with investigative methodology, not predatory instinct.
issues.fix: I walked through the mansion turning off lights. Collecting the cameras Josh had found. Straightening the furniture we'd knocked over. Cleaning up the mess we'd made while the real damage remained untouched.
issues.rationale: 'Cleaning up the mess' is neutralΓÇöcould reference literal disorder or relationship damage. 'Real damage remained untouched' focuses on emotional aftermath rather than evidence management.

issues.line_text:
From my window, lights glowed in the mansion. Josh moving past windows. Pacing. Probably reviewing his own surveillance footage, building his case against me, convincing himself he was the hunter and I was the predator.

The irony would be funny if it wasn't so tragic.

issues.fix:
From my window, lights glowed in the mansion. Josh moving past windows. Pacing. Probably reviewing his own surveillance footage, building his case against me, convincing himself he'd figured me out.

issues.line_text: And the pattern was accelerating. The episodes coming closer together. The stress and isolation amplifying something I still didn't fully understand.
issues.description: Eleanor tracking 'the pattern' and 'episodes' in clinical terms reveals she's monitoring Josh's fugue statesΓÇöinvestigator behavior. 'Still didn't fully understand' reveals she's seeking to understand his condition, not to hurt him.
issues.fix: And he was falling apart faster now. The cracks showing more often. The stress and isolation breaking down whatever control he'd been clinging to.
issues.rationale: 'Falling apart' + 'cracks showing' + 'breaking down control' can read as Eleanor watching Josh weaken (predatory satisfaction at prey's vulnerability). Removes clinical pattern-tracking language.

issues.line_text: SoonΓÇömaybe days, maybe hoursΓÇösomething would break. And when it did, I'd have to decide what to do with everything I knew.
issues.description: 'Everything I knew' reveals Eleanor possesses knowledge/evidenceΓÇöinvestigator position. The phrasing implies she'll make a decision based on information (investigative methodology), not predatory impulse.
issues.fix: SoonΓÇömaybe days, maybe hoursΓÇösomething would break. And when it did, I'd have to finish what I came here to do.
issues.rationale: 'Finish what I came here to do' is predatory closure languageΓÇöreaders think she means to harm Josh. Actually refers to confronting him with evidence. Removes the knowledge-based decision framing.

issues.description: 'Certainty I'd started with' reveals Eleanor began with conviction (investigative certainty about Josh's guilt) that's now wavering. Predators don't start with 'certainty'ΓÇöthey act on desire/compulsion.
issues.fix: I was out of time. Out of options. Out of the control I thought I had.

issues.line_text: All I had left was the questions, the fading weeks of my own life, and a man who loved me while suspecting I was trying to destroy him.
issues.description: 'The questions' reveals Eleanor is seeking answersΓÇöinvestigator motivation. Combined with 'fading weeks of my own life,' this comes dangerously close to revealing her terminal illness before the planned reveal.
